plan_quotes.community_vision: Montgomery County aspires to transition from a suburban bedroom community into an interconnected, economically competitive, and racially integrated jurisdiction. The county's vision centers on compact, corridor-focused development that fosters walkable 'Complete Communities' and '15-minute living' while preserving its Agricultural Reserve. The plan prioritizes addressing historical racial and economic inequities, improving environmental resilience, and integrating design, arts, and culture into the daily lives of all residents.
geographic_addresses: 2425 Reedie Drive, Wheaton, MD
Connecticut Avenue & Manor Road, Kensington, MD
University Boulevard & New Hampshire Avenue, Silver Spring, MD
Seven Locks Road & River Road, Bethesda, MD

quotes.text: The establishment of the residential wedge consigned more than one-third of the county to zoning exclusively for single-family homes, leaving many of our neighborhoods reliant on automobiles and disconnected from many amenities and services.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights that dedicating more than one-third of the county to exclusive single-family zoning left many neighborhoods isolated, signaling a key opportunity to introduce missing middle housing and mixed-use options that better connect residents to daily amenities.

quotes.text: By concentrating more housing of different sizes and types near high-quality transit corridors, we can provide housing that will help keep the most productive workers in the county, curb escalating prices in the most desirable locations, and improve accessibility of jobs, transportation, and services while being mindful not to displace current residents.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support a growing workforce, planning officials recommend concentrating more housing of different sizes and types near high-quality transit corridors to keep housing attainable, improve transit access, and avoid displacement.

quotes.text: Existing suburban office parks in locations such as Rock Spring or Clarksburg’s COMSAT site have large existing buildings that can accommodate employment but lack the integration of uses, services, and amenities necessary to succeed in an increasingly competitive office market.
quotes.briefing_quote: The document notes that aging suburban office parks can be successfully repositioned through infill and redevelopment to integrate housing, retail, and public spaces, creating the vibrant mixed-use environments that modern employers and residents seek.

quotes.text: Adding more 'Missing Middle' housing types – ranging from low to medium densities such as accessory dwelling units (ADUs); duplexes; triplexes; quadplexes; live-work units; and clustered housing such as townhouses, courtyard dwellings and smaller apartment buildings to more neighborhoods is intended to provide more choice, enhance intergenerational interaction, promote aging in place, and build social capital.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan emphasizes the value of adding 'Missing Middle' housing types to more neighborhoods—including duplexes, triplexes, and townhomes—to expand residential choice, build social capital, and facilitate aging in place.

quotes.text: Can't take my ladder on the Purple Line.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local working-class resident cautioned planners about transit-focused changes, stating, 'Can’t take my ladder on the Purple Line,' illustrating the critical need to preserve vehicle-accessible corridors and parking for service providers.

community_organizations: Arts & Humanities Council of Montgomery County

plan_quotes.community_vision: Rockville will be a vibrant, multicultural, and socio-economically inclusive city with distinct neighborhoods that are supported by a strong local economy, a healthy natural environment, and a desirable quality of life founded on a responsive government.
geographic_addresses: Rockville Pike & Halpine Road, Rockville, MD
Veirs Mill Road & First Street, Rockville, MD
North Washington Street & Hungerford Drive, Rockville, MD
East Middle Lane & Maryland Avenue, Rockville, MD
West Montgomery Avenue & Mannakee Street, Rockville, MD
Park Road & North Stonestreet Avenue, Rockville, MD

quotes.text: Given that most new residential growth in the city will come in the form of multiple unit residential buildings, as apartments or condominiums, and that not all locations are appropriate for mixed-use development, Rockville needs a higher density residential zone.
quotes.briefing_quote: To accommodate evolving multi-family housing demands, the plan notes that "most new residential growth in the city will come in the form of multiple unit residential buildings, as apartments or condominiums, and that not all locations are appropriate for mixed-use development, Rockville needs a higher density residential zone."

quotes.text: One way to accommodate more affordable housing options, flexible space for an office or shared family living arrangements, and financial assistance for current homeowners, while maintaining the city’s predominantly residential character, is with accessory apartments and accessory dwelling units.
quotes.briefing_quote: To address affordability while maintaining neighborhood fabric, the plan highlights that "one way to accommodate more affordable housing options, flexible space for an office or shared family living arrangements, and financial assistance for current homeowners, while maintaining the city’s predominantly residential character, is with accessory apartments and accessory dwelling units."

quotes.text: Steady additions of commercial and amenity space on the ground floor of new buildings bring the opportunity for new shops and restaurants, supported by new residential units and offices on upper floors. This Plan promotes an intensification of development that encourages an active street scene and vibrant commercial district.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support local businesses and create active downtown corridors, the plan outlines that "steady additions of commercial and amenity space on the ground floor of new buildings bring the opportunity for new shops and restaurants, supported by new residential units and offices on upper floors."

quotes.text: These 'missing middle' housing types, also discussed in the Land Use Element, include: Duplexes; Triplexes; Fourplexes or quads; Sixplexes; Townhouses or rowhouses; Small apartment buildings; and Garden apartments. These housing types are largely missing in American suburbs, including Rockville, in part because land use policies and zoning do not allow their type of construction in single-unit detached residential zones...
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan identifies the need for diversified housing forms, noting that "these 'missing middle' housing types... are largely missing in American suburbs, including Rockville, in part because land use policies and zoning do not allow their type of construction in single-unit detached residential zones."

quotes.text: The most successful office clusters in Montgomery County are part of mixed-use development with a strong sense of place and quality environment. Transit connectivity is increasingly important to office tenants.
quotes.briefing_quote: Citing a countywide office market assessment, the plan underscores that "the most successful office clusters in Montgomery County are part of mixed-use development with a strong sense of place and quality environment. Transit connectivity is increasingly important to office tenants."

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

quotes.text: All new rental housing should be mixed-income, meaning that it must be accessible to people making all ranges of income (from no income to unrestricted income). Each new development should be 1/3 low-income units, 1/3 workforce units, and 1/3 units for unrestricted income renters where economically feasible.
quotes.briefing_quote: To promote socioeconomic diversity and inclusivity, the plan stresses that 'all new rental housing should be mixed-income... each new development should be 1/3 low-income units, 1/3 workforce units, and 1/3 units for unrestricted income renters where economically feasible.'

quotes.text: Many of the existing rowhouses in Cherry Hill are roughly 750—900 SF and have 2-3 bedrooms, with 1 full bathroom. Families today are looking for 3 and 4-bedrooms with at least 2 to 2.5 bathrooms;... Shorter lengths of rowhouses (duplexes, triplexes, and 4-unit buildings) would help to break up the streets and provide green between the buildings.
quotes.briefing_quote: To mitigate out-migration of families seeking larger spaces, the plan highlights a strong demand for developers to build 'larger houses with contemporary floor plans' featuring three to four bedrooms and multiple bathrooms.

quotes.text: Cherry Hill currently does not have the spending required to support a supermarket and would need to capture additional demand from surrounding areas... The best way to address residents' needs for groceries is to implement a phased approach.
quotes.briefing_quote: Acknowledging that the area's current spending power sits below national grocery chain thresholds, the plan recommends that developers 'attract a small, private grocery chain or family-owned franchise' as part of a phased food security approach.

quotes.text: In the future, a mixed-use Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) neighborhood may be possible next to the existing Cherry Hill Light RailLink station... quotes.briefing_quote: The planning team identified a major opportunity to create a 'vibrant mixed-use Transit-Oriented Development neighborhood next to the existing Cherry Hill Light RailLink station' to integrate higher-density housing and local retail.

quotes.text: The approved One Westport development plans include a combination of residential and commercial uses, alongside a public waterfront trail and park spaces.

quotes.text: The layout builds on recommendations of the 2020 Cherry Hill Transformation Plan and includes new equitable mixed-use development on vacant land between Hanover and Potee Streets and south of Potee. quotes.briefing_quote: To better serve neighborhood needs, planners recommend "new equitable mixed-use development on vacant land... [including] a combination of mixed-income housing, healthcare, and a grocery store" along the Hanover-Potee Corridor.

quotes.text: The buildings’ bulk and form are envisioned as low to mid-rise and mixed-use: at most three to four stories of residential over a base of commercial-retail or professional services.

quotes.text: The Plan recommends establishing a native plant nursery, managed and staffed by South Baltimore residents, to supply park improvement projects and Middle Branch communities with locally grown plants and locally made building materials.

quotes.text: The Plan recommends establishing a storefront marketplace that will offer the opportunity to activate the waterfront by drawing local residents and visitors to purchase culturally authentic goods, art, and foods from an assortment of vendors.

quotes.text: At the north lot, a visible and well-connected site near the base of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Bridge, the Plan suggests two alternatives – a civic use, such as library or other community facility, or a low-scale commercial development to support the community and the hospital and bring more activity to the waterfront.
quotes.briefing_quote: For underutilized parking areas near MedStar Harbor Hospital, the plan suggests "a civic use, such as [a] library or other community facility, or a low-scale commercial development to support the community and the hospital" while driving active street life.

quotes.text: catalyzing investments in larger, mixed-use or multi-family housing developments with crucial pre-development or gap funding

quotes.text: The 2020 Cherry Hill Transformation Plan identifies key sites for development in Cherry Hill, as well as locations for new housing, active corridors, and economic initiatives.

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

plan_quotes.community_vision: Cultivate investment and hope in the Oliver Neighborhood through creating visible connections between resilient green spaces, activated cultural assets, and vibrant community resources. Oliver aspires to transition from a historically rich but currently underinvested neighborhood characterized by high vacancy into a thriving, safe, and walkable community that balances historic single-family rowhouses with targeted multifamily and mixed-use density, particularly along the Harford Avenue and North Avenue corridors.
geographic_addresses: North Avenue & Broadway, Baltimore, MD
Biddle Street & Broadway, Baltimore, MD
Biddle Street & Ensor Street, Baltimore, MD
North Avenue & Ensor Street, Baltimore, MD
Harford Avenue & Oliver Street, Baltimore, MD
Central Avenue & Hoffman Street, Baltimore, MD

quotes.text: The Family Dollar store site at the corner of Oliver St. and Harford Ave. lies at a critical intersection at the historic heart of the neighborhood. Given this prominent location, we should reimagine the Family Dollar store site in the long-term as a multi-family development consistent with underlying zoning with community-serving retail and active ground floor frontages on the streets, with integrated podium parking underneath
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights a prime redevelopment opportunity at the corner of Oliver Street and Harford Avenue, recommending that stakeholders "reimagine the Family Dollar store site in the long-term as a multi-family development consistent with underlying zoning with community-serving retail and active ground floor frontages" to anchor the heart of the community.

quotes.text: Harford Ave. between Federal and Biddle Street, (Mixed-use Residential/Multi-Family Housing/ Commercial) to feature a few mid-rise mixed-use multifamily buildings with ground-floor retail that can support a grocery store or smaller businesses such as coffee shops, apparel, bank, nail salons, etc. with a minimum of 85% of the units being market rate
quotes.briefing_quote: To support local economic viability and house new neighbors, the community visualizes Harford Avenue hosting "mid-rise mixed-use multifamily buildings with ground-floor retail that can support a grocery store or smaller businesses... with a minimum of 85% of the units being market rate."

quotes.text: All single family infill (new construction) should not exceed three stories and, while not yet officially designated as a CHAP district, should generally attempt to align to the design standards presented in the City's CHAP guidelines to best protect the historic character of Oliver.
quotes.briefing_quote: To preserve the aesthetic integrity of the area, the plan requests that "all single family infill (new construction) should not exceed three stories" and should design-align with the Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation guidelines.

quotes.text: The high concentration of vacant land in this focus area holds Oliver’s best potential to attract multi-family development consistent with underlying zoning into the community.
quotes.briefing_quote: Addressing the high vacancy along the western boundary, planners note that the area holds "Oliver's best potential to attract multi-family development consistent with underlying zoning into the community" as a mechanism for neighborhood growth.

quotes.text: Current zoning in Oliver makes it challenging for development to be concentrated and responsive to community needs and desires. To support continued investment and development for small businesses and renovations that strengthen the fabric of the community, zoning practices will need to be re-considered.
quotes.briefing_quote: Local development partner ReBUILD Metro pointed out that "current zoning in Oliver makes it challenging for development to be concentrated and responsive to community needs," indicating a vital opportunity for zoning realignment to foster neighborhood-serving storefronts.

quotes.text: I hope that Oliver is a thriving neighborhood. As a native Baltimorean that recently returned to invest in the city, I chose this neighborhood but sometimes have regrets. I love my property but the neighborhood feels stagnant. There doesn’t appear to be a plan, but spotty investment that feels disconnected. Given its location to a major hub like JHH and downtown the neighborhood has potential yet its unrealized.
quotes.briefing_quote: A returning native resident highlighted the gap between hope and reality, stating that while they love their property, "the neighborhood feels stagnant" with disconnected investments, emphasizing that its proximity to downtown and major employment hubs represents major "unrealized potential."

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.
geographic_addresses: Forge Road & Belair Road, Perry Hall, MD
Compass Road & Wampler Road, Middle River, MD
Cowenton Avenue & Pulaski Highway, White Marsh, MD
Rolling Road & Windsor Mill Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Rolling Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Old Court Road, Randallstown, MD
Wharf Road, Sparrows Point, MD

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.

quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.

quotes.text: The Family Dollar store site at the corner of Oliver St. and Harford Ave. lies at a critical intersection at the historic heart of the neighborhood. quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights a prime redevelopment opportunity at the corner of Oliver Street and Harford Avenue, recommending that stakeholders "reimagine the Family Dollar store site in the long-term as a multi-family development consistent with underlying zoning with community-serving retail and active ground floor frontages" to anchor the heart of the community.

quotes.text: Harford Ave. between Federal and Biddle Street, (Mixed-use Residential/Multi-Family Housing/ Commercial) to feature a few mid-rise mixed-use multifamily buildings with ground-floor retail that can support a grocery store or smaller businesses such as coffee shops, apparel, bank, nail salons, etc. with a minimum of 85% of the units being market rate
quotes.briefing_quote: To support local economic viability and house new neighbors, the community visualizes Harford Avenue hosting "mid-rise mixed-use multifamily buildings with ground-floor retail that can support a grocery store or smaller businesses... with a minimum of 85% of the units being market rate."

quotes.text: All single family infill (new construction) should not exceed three stories and, while not yet officially designated as a CHAP district, should generally attempt to align to the design standards presented in the City's CHAP guidelines to best protect the historic character of Oliver.

quotes.text: The high concentration of vacant land in this focus area holds Oliver’s best potential to attract multi-family development consistent with underlying zoning into the community.
quotes.briefing_quote: Addressing the high vacancy along the western boundary, planners note that the area holds "Oliver's best potential to attract multi-family development consistent with underlying zoning into the community" as a mechanism for neighborhood growth.

quotes.text: Current zoning in Oliver makes it challenging for development to be concentrated and responsive to community needs and desires. To support continued investment and development for small businesses and renovations that strengthen the fabric of the community, zoning practices will need to be re-considered.
quotes.briefing_quote: Local development partner ReBUILD Metro pointed out that "current zoning in Oliver makes it challenging for development to be concentrated and responsive to community needs," indicating a vital opportunity for zoning realignment to foster neighborhood-serving storefronts.

quotes.text: I hope that Oliver is a thriving neighborhood. As a native Baltimorean that recently returned to invest in the city, I chose this neighborhood but sometimes have regrets. Given its location to a major hub like JHH and downtown the neighborhood has potential yet its unrealized.
quotes.briefing_quote: A returning native resident highlighted the gap between hope and reality, stating that while they love their property, "the neighborhood feels stagnant" with disconnected investments, emphasizing that its proximity to downtown and major employment hubs represents major "unrealized potential."

quotes.text: The FLUM focuses new growth into redevelopment areas, which account for approximately 1.5% of the County's already-developed land. This approach addresses high demand for housing and commercial growth.
quotes.briefing_quote: To sustainably manage growth, the plan targets redevelopment on just 1.5% of the County's developed land to balance housing and commercial demands.

quotes.text: Pedestrian safety must be improved—I keep seeing pedestrians walking down the middle of Broken Land or Snowden because there’s no reasonable public transit or walking paths for them to safely get where they’re going.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local workshop participant emphasized that pedestrian safety must be improved on Broken Land Parkway and Snowden River Parkway by providing better walking paths and transit options.

quotes.text: Boosting commercial-base development is one of the most promising strategies to help rebalance the expenditure needs and fiscal resources. The County should continue to build on its current strengths in developing and implementing comprehensive strategies to promote, retain, and expand its commercial base.
quotes.briefing_quote: The Spending Affordability Advisory Committee emphasized that boosting commercial-base development is critical to balancing the County's long-term fiscal resources.

quotes.text: The concept of missing middle housing is referenced throughout the Plan. It is a housing strategy that is intended to create more diverse housing opportunities for our increasingly socioeconomically diverse County.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan promotes missing middle housing to create more diverse housing opportunities that remain compatible in scale with surrounding neighborhoods.

quotes.text: Many developed areas of Howard County are zoned for single-family detached homes. quotes.briefing_quote: The plan identifies potential for modest single-family infill, noting some neighborhoods could be further subdivided under existing zoning to add homes of similar size.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Catonsville-Patapsco community envisions a sustainable, well-connected, and culturally vibrant future. Key aspirations include expanding the local arts ecosystem through the newly designated Catonsville Arts and Entertainment District along Frederick Road, improving active transportation and trail connectivity via groups like Catonsville Rails to Trails, and preserving watershed resources near Patapsco Valley State Park. The community aims to revitalize legacy neighborhoods, address commercial vacancies, and expand quality housing choices—including affordable housing partnerships and accessory dwelling units (ADUs)—while navigating existing low-density zoning constraints that historically limit larger-scale infill development.

quotes.text: Scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger scale new development or infill
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan notes a 'scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger-scale new development or infill,' highlighting the critical importance of strategic infill projects.

quotes.text: Barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs).
quotes.briefing_quote: The assessment identifies clear 'barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs)' that must be navigated to successfully introduce multi-family and mixed-use options.

quotes.text: The majority of zoning in the Catonsville SC area is low density residential, that primarily supports single family development. ... The current residential zoning in the majority of the SC Area does not easily support higher density development.
quotes.briefing_quote: Planning staff emphasized that 'the majority of zoning in the Catonsville Sustainable Community Area is low density residential, which primarily supports single family development' and does not easily accommodate higher density development styles.

quotes.text: Zoning changes occur through the County’s CZMP process... several of these requests for change were denied, though a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144.
quotes.briefing_quote: Recent comprehensive zoning reviews show progress, noting that while some requests were denied, 'a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144' to align with main street commercial revitalization goals.

quotes.text: Support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the SC area through the development process and policy development.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community intends to 'support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the Sustainable Community Area through the development process and policy development' to broaden localized residential choices.

plan_quotes.community_vision: Ellicott City aspires to preserve its unique historic character and environmental setting while systematically mitigating severe flood risks along its core watershed. The community seeks to revitalize its historic Main Street and West End through creative economic development, adaptive reuse of public assets like the historic courthouse, and environmentally sustainable infill developments like mixed-income housing, balancing heritage preservation with modern climate resilience.

quotes.text: Explore opportunities for in-town residential uses within the walkable core. Residential use is essential for an authentic and vibrant walkable community.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan emphasizes that planning officials should "explore opportunities for in-town residential uses within the walkable core" because "residential use is essential for an authentic and vibrant walkable community."

quotes.text: Burgess Mill Station II is one of the largest infill developments in the SC area. The Burgess Mill project added a 53-home mixed-income apartment option for prospective residents on the south side of Ellicott Mills Drive and the Station II just around the corner off Fels Lane.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights successful local housing models, noting that "Burgess Mill Station II is one of the largest infill developments in the Sustainable Community area," which successfully "added a 53-home mixed-income apartment option for prospective residents."

quotes.text: Housing affordability remains a challenge in the sustainable community and across the region. Steep elevations and lack of available land for greenfield development limits future infill development opportunities.
quotes.briefing_quote: Recognizing geographic and regulatory constraints, the plan notes that "housing affordability remains a challenge" in Ellicott City, where "steep elevations and lack of available land for greenfield development limits future infill development opportunities"—presenting a critical opportunity for creative, well-designed pocket developments.

quotes.text: The Department of Public Works has petitioned the Zoning Board to rezone the now-vacant Historic Courthouse and associated properties from Historic Office (HO) to Historic Commercial (HC) to encourage a range of possible reuse opportunities.
quotes.briefing_quote: To spur economic vitality, the plan details that the county petitioned to "rezone the now-vacant Historic Courthouse and associated properties from Historic Office to Historic Commercial" to actively encourage a flexible range of possible adaptive reuse opportunities.

quotes.text: While a variety of uses could be considered for the property, they should be determined as part of the disposition process, based upon market conditions and feasibility. Proposed uses should be complementary to the Main Street business community, and the form of new structures should be sensitive to the historic district. The process to create the ECMP included unique hotel/accommodations, apartments, office space and/or business incubator space.
quotes.briefing_quote: For the redevelopment of the prominent Courthouse site, the plan advises that "proposed uses should be complementary to the Main Street business community, and the form of new structures should be sensitive to the historic district," with prior community planning processes for the Ellicott City Watershed Master Plan identifying "unique hotel/accommodations, apartments, office space and/or business incubator space" as desired options.

quotes.text: Explore the opportunity for a food hall or creative food establishment within the core, as the market study indicates that opportunities for food-related retail is significant.
quotes.briefing_quote: In seeking to expand the district's retail mix, planning documents urge developers to "explore the opportunity for a food hall or creative food establishment within the core," driven by market research indicating that "opportunities for food-related retail is significant."

quotes.text: The establishment of the residential wedge consigned more than one-third of the county to zoning exclusively for single-family homes, leaving many of our neighborhoods reliant on automobiles and disconnected from many amenities and services.

quotes.text: By concentrating more housing of different sizes and types near high-quality transit corridors, we can provide housing that will help keep the most productive workers in the county, curb escalating prices in the most desirable locations, and improve accessibility of jobs, transportation, and services while being mindful not to displace current residents.

quotes.text: Existing suburban office parks in locations such as Rock Spring or Clarksburg’s COMSAT site have large existing buildings that can accommodate employment but lack the integration of uses, services, and amenities necessary to succeed in an increasingly competitive office market.
quotes.briefing_quote: The document notes that aging suburban office parks can be successfully repositioned through infill and redevelopment to integrate housing, retail, and public spaces, creating the vibrant mixed-use environments that modern employers and residents seek.

quotes.text: Adding more 'Missing Middle' housing types – ranging from low to medium densities such as accessory dwelling units (ADUs); duplexes; triplexes; quadplexes; live-work units; and clustered housing such as townhouses, courtyard dwellings and smaller apartment buildings to more neighborhoods is intended to provide more choice, enhance intergenerational interaction, promote aging in place, and build social capital.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan emphasizes the value of adding 'Missing Middle' housing types to more neighborhoods—including duplexes, triplexes, and townhomes—to expand residential choice, build social capital, and facilitate aging in place.

quotes.text: Can't take my ladder on the Purple Line.

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The City of Frederick's vision, driven by its CommUNITY 2030 Strategic Plan and 2020 Comprehensive Plan, focuses on sustainable, equitable development across three distinct corridors: Downtown, the Golden Mile, and East Frederick. The community seeks to revitalize underutilized commercial areas and preserve its historic character through selective redevelopment, adaptive reuse, and strategic infill. Key goals include diversifying and increasing housing options (especially affordable and multi-family residential units), enhancing multi-modal transportation systems with shared-use paths, implementing form-based codes to encourage vibrant mixed-use environments, and fostering robust public-private collaborations to ensure high quality of life for all residents.

plan_quotes.community_vision: Leonardtown aspires to be a family-friendly, independent business, and restaurant hub in St. Mary's County, offering a distinct sense of place centered amidst water, nature, and cultural-based assets. The community seeks to maintain a vibrant environment for residents and visitors by leveraging public and private investments, enhancing pedestrian walkability, expanding waterfront amenities, and providing a diverse range of housing choices.

quotes.text: The growth of the waterfront, with its 2.5 miles of shoreline, and expansion westerly will bring opportunities for additional types of housing. An exciting addition to Leonardtown's future housing prospects is the area just west of Lawrence Avenue (the Tudor Hall Property), which is slated for an assortment of housing including garden apartments, townhomes, small single-family lots, and mixed-use housing above retail shops.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan notes that expansion west of Lawrence Avenue onto the Tudor Hall Property represents an exciting opportunity to introduce 'an assortment of housing including garden apartments, townhomes, small single-family lots, and mixed-use housing above retail shops' to bridge the waterfront and the downtown area.

quotes.text: Within the Sustainable Community Area several buildings have been converted to mixed-use residential/commercial buildings. Thus providing much needed housing in the downtown area and keeping people in the area after businesses close, providing 'eyes on the streets' after dark and built in customers for downtown businesses
quotes.briefing_quote: Municipal organizers reported that converting downtown structures to mixed-use buildings has successfully provided 'much needed housing in the downtown area and keeping people in the area after businesses close, providing "eyes on the streets" after dark and built-in customers for downtown businesses.'

quotes.text: Even though progress has been made, Leonardtown would like to increase the number of retail businesses in the Sustainable Community Area.
quotes.briefing_quote: The 2023 renewal application emphasizes that despite healthy commercial development, the community seeks to 'increase the number of retail businesses' within the Sustainable Community Area, specifically targeting a retail recruitment strategy.

quotes.text: While progress has been made, the Town needs to continue to work with developers to increase affordable housing, over 55 housing, and continue work on making redevelopment process easier as with PIRO overlay zoning district.
quotes.briefing_quote: The Town highlights an ongoing opportunity to 'work with developers to increase affordable housing [and] over 55 housing' while simplifying the approval process using tools like the Planned Infill and Redevelopment District overlay.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The overall vision for the Comprehensive Plan is to maintain the historical character of Leonardtown while embracing growth that is occurring in and around the Town's municipal boundary. By utilizing land use and growth management practices based on shared principles agreed upon by residents and Town Officials, Leonardtown aims to achieve balanced development that protects its small-town charm while ensuring it remains the core hub for St. Mary's County's government, education, health services, and judicial systems.

quotes.briefing_quote: To address local housing needs, the plan highlights the opportunity to "support the development of duplexes, small lot homes, and townhomes, especially within growth areas like Tudor Hall Farm, to increase density while maintaining affordability."

quotes.text: Promote mixed-use zoning in the Downtown Central Business District (CBD) and other appropriate locations, encouraging residences above commercial spaces to foster business support and community activity beyond business hours.

quotes.text: Pursue the long-standing objective of establishing a full-service hotel in St. Mary’s County that offers amenities for both business and leisure travelers.

quotes.briefing_quote: Although the town is built out, the plan highlights that "due to zoning changes, there is some possibility of mixed-use residential in the industrial area" if transitioning grandfathered businesses close.

quotes.text: Conflicting views in the community about redevelopment of existing homes.
quotes.briefing_quote: When evaluating residential infill, developers should anticipate "conflicting views in the community about redevelopment of existing homes."

quotes.text: Current lot sizes of industrial property especially lack depth needed for significant redevelopment opportunities.
quotes.briefing_quote: Physical site planning may prove challenging because "current lot sizes of industrial property especially lack depth needed for significant redevelopment opportunities."

community_organizations: Walkable Bikeable Berwyn Heights Task Force
Boys and Girls Club of America
Citizens Commission on Quality of Life

plan_quotes.community_vision: Greenbelt strives to enhance its unique co-op heritage and National Historic Landmark identity while expanding economic vitality, environmental stewardship, and multi-modal transit options. The community aims to sustainably manage its ecological footprint, protect its extensive forest preserves, and revitalize underutilized commercial corridors, while actively advocating for affordable housing and multi-family residential opportunities to create a more walkable, equitable, and vibrant future.
geographic_addresses: 25 Crescent Road, Greenbelt, MD
Cherrywood Lane, Greenbelt, MD
Southway, Greenbelt, MD
Greenbelt Road, Greenbelt, MD

quotes.text: Due to a number of challenges, the City has been unable to increase its inventory of affordable housing since its designation as a Sustainable Community. Prince George’s County lacks incentive programs or affordable housing requirements tied to development like other surrounding counties, and this makes it more difficult to attract developers to Greenbelt to construct an affordable housing product even though the demand for affordable housing remains.
quotes.briefing_quote: City planners highlighted that although "the demand for affordable housing remains," the lack of county-level incentive programs "makes it more difficult to attract developers to Greenbelt to construct an affordable housing product," presenting an open opportunity for collaborative public-private partnerships.

quotes.text: Promote infill development and other redevelopment options for underutilized residential or commercial lots.
quotes.briefing_quote: The Sustainable Communities Action Plan outlines a strategy to "promote infill development and other redevelopment options for underutilized residential or commercial lots," creating clear pathways for adaptive reuse and compact development.

quotes.text: Opportunities for new multi-family residential development
quotes.briefing_quote: The city's housing assessment identifies "opportunities for new multi-family residential development" as a key strength to accommodate growing housing demands near major transit assets.

quotes.text: Oversee the conveyance of indoor recreation space to the City as part of the redevelopment plans of Beltway Plaza.
quotes.briefing_quote: The city's active planning goals include a strategy to "oversee the conveyance of indoor recreation space to the City as part of the redevelopment plans" of the Beltway Plaza site, fostering integrated mixed-use environments.

community_organizations: Greenbelt’s Advisory Committee on Environmental Sustainability (Green ACES)

plan_quotes.community_vision: The City of College Park envisions a diverse, vibrant, connected, and economically successful university community. By partnering with the University of Maryland, the community seeks to stabilize and preserve historic neighborhoods, foster smart growth and transit-oriented development, expand housing diversity, support locally owned businesses, and champion environmental sustainability and climate resilience.
geographic_addresses: 7401 Baltimore Avenue, College Park, MD
9219 51st Avenue, College Park, MD
Cherokee Street & 48th Place, College Park, MD
Greenbelt Road & Rhode Island Avenue, College Park, MD
7308 Yale Avenue, College Park, MD

quotes.text: Development has been stalled in this area due to an outdated plan that did not truly promote transit-oriented development. A new Transit District Development Plan was adopted by Prince George’s County in 2015 and prospects have improved. A WMATA joint development project was approved for 400 apartment units and 10,000 SF of retail and County owned property across from the Metro station is being sold for mixed-use development.
quotes.briefing_quote: While past development near the Metro station was hindered by outdated zoning, the adoption of a new Transit District Development Plan has unlocked major opportunities, including an approved project featuring "400 apartment units and 10,000 square feet of retail" alongside county-owned property slated for transit-oriented mixed-use development.

quotes.text: The City has approved 10 new multifamily/townhouse projects since 2017 amounting to an increase of 2,626 dwelling units. About a dozen single-family home infill development has occurred. ... Most new development in College Park is redevelopment of commercial corridors and centers.
quotes.briefing_quote: Indicating a strong market preference for higher-density redevelopment in commercial areas, the plan notes that "the City has approved 10 new multifamily/townhouse projects since 2017" representing an addition of 2,626 dwelling units.

quotes.text: Strengthen College Park neighborhoods by reducing the number of single-family homes that are converted to group rental properties by continuing to offer homeownership grant programs, establishing a community land trust, and exploring new programs for housing rehabilitation with Habitat for Humanity Maryland.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community aims to stabilize residential areas, seeking to "strengthen College Park neighborhoods by reducing the number of single-family homes that are converted to group rental properties" through the creation of a community land trust and targeted homeownership programs.

quotes.text: Use recently acquired property on Calvert Road for the development of missing middle housing.
quotes.briefing_quote: To promote housing type diversity, community planning goals advise the city to "use recently acquired property on Calvert Road for the development of missing middle housing" as a bridge between low- and high-density neighborhoods.

quotes.text: Many long-term businesses have closed or have been relocated due to new development. ARPA assistance was provided to many businesses and has helped, but high rents are making it difficult for local, independent businesses to survive and for other to enter the market.
quotes.briefing_quote: Highlighting a clear opportunity for developers to build affordable storefront spaces, the plan notes that "high rents are making it difficult for local, independent businesses to survive and for others to enter the market" amid ongoing corridor redevelopment.

quotes.text: Route 1 has seen tremendous redevelopment activity since being rezoned from C-S-C (Commercial Shopping Center) to M-U-I (Mixed-Use Infill) in 2001 and is successfully transforming from a strip commercial corridor to a mixed-use boulevard with a series of walkable nodes
quotes.briefing_quote: Due to progressive zoning changes, the US Route 1 corridor is "successfully transforming from a strip commercial corridor to a mixed-use boulevard with a series of walkable nodes" that enhance local economic vibrancy.

community_organizations: College Park Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee
College Park Committee for a Better Environment

properties.tract_name: The neighborhoods of West Glen and Powhatan

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.
geographic_addresses: Forge Road & Belair Road, Perry Hall, MD
Compass Road & Wampler Road, Middle River, MD
Cowenton Avenue & Pulaski Highway, White Marsh, MD
Rolling Road & Windsor Mill Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Rolling Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Old Court Road, Randallstown, MD
Wharf Road, Sparrows Point, MD

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

community_organizations: Set the Captives Free Outreach, Worship and Education (OWE) Center

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Northwest Gateways community seeks to enhance its overall economic vitality, neighborhood livability, and environmental health by pursuing a vision of improved streetscapes, commercial corridor revitalization, and diverse housing options. By leveraging sustainable community programs and targeted public investments, the area strives to foster commercial growth, address transportation and pedestrian connectivity gaps, and build active, safe, and attractive neighborhoods where families of all backgrounds can thrive.
geographic_addresses: Liberty Road & Offutt Road, Randallstown, MD
Rolling Road & Windsor Mill Road, Woodlawn, MD
Hooks Lane & Reisterstown Road, Pikesville, MD
Dolfield Blvd & Red Run Blvd, Owings Mills, MD
Old Court Road & Carlson Lane, Pikesville, MD

quotes.text: There is currently an affordable housing proposal within the Pikesville CRD that is requesting rezoning to support multi-family apartments.
quotes.briefing_quote: In the Pikesville Commercial Revitalization District, there is an affordable housing proposal requesting rezoning to support multi-family apartments, showing local momentum for adding density.

quotes.text: There has not been demolition of blighted properties in the area. However, there is an interest from the County to assemble vacant commercial properties on Liberty Rd to assist CDCs in redevelopment. In addition, there is discussion to redevelop the old International House of Pancakes and Bennigan's restaurants located in front of Security Square mall.
quotes.briefing_quote: The county is looking to assemble vacant commercial properties along Liberty Road to assist community development corporations in redevelopment, with further discussions centered on redeveloping the former restaurant sites in front of Security Square Mall.

quotes.text: Expand full spectrum housing for residents at diverse income levels and life stages and for individuals with disabilities by encouraging high quality mixed income, multigenerational developments. Promote Housing Accessibility Modification programs to make housing more accessible. Continue to implement smart growth policies by supporting mixed-use development and Traditional Neighborhood Development in the area.
quotes.briefing_quote: Planning guidelines emphasize the need to encourage high-quality mixed-income, multigenerational developments while supporting smart growth policies such as mixed-use and Traditional Neighborhood Development.

quotes.text: Some homes in Colonial Village have been improved. There are homes in the Pikesville area that have gone through the zoning petition process for additions. This is largely attributed to growing families that require additional space and secondary kitchens due to religious food preparation requirements.
quotes.briefing_quote: In Pikesville, growing families are actively seeking zoning petitions for home additions and secondary kitchens to meet specific cultural and religious food preparation needs.

quotes.text: Lack of quality retail and chain restaurants in the Liberty Rd CRD... Lack of variety of businesses to meet the needs of the community... Abundance of unwanted businesses... Businesses closing and vacant gas stations are an eyesore to the residents
quotes.briefing_quote: Community feedback highlights a lack of quality retail and restaurant variety along the Liberty Road Commercial Revitalization District, alongside concerns over vacant storefronts and gas stations.

community_organizations: Pikesville-Owings Mills Regional Chamber of Commerce
Middle Gwynns Falls SWAP Steering Committee

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Catonsville-Patapsco community envisions a sustainable, well-connected, and culturally vibrant future. Key aspirations include expanding the local arts ecosystem through the newly designated Catonsville Arts and Entertainment District along Frederick Road, improving active transportation and trail connectivity via groups like Catonsville Rails to Trails, and preserving watershed resources near Patapsco Valley State Park. The community aims to revitalize legacy neighborhoods, address commercial vacancies, and expand quality housing choices—including affordable housing partnerships and accessory dwelling units (ADUs)—while navigating existing low-density zoning constraints that historically limit larger-scale infill development.
geographic_addresses: Ingleside Ave & Edmondson Ave, Catonsville, MD
Ingleside Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD
Maidens Choice Lane & Kenwood Ave, Catonsville, MD
S. Paradise Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD
Mellor Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD
Winters Lane & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD

quotes.text: Scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger scale new development or infill
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan notes a 'scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger-scale new development or infill,' highlighting the critical importance of strategic infill projects.

quotes.text: Barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs).
quotes.briefing_quote: The assessment identifies clear 'barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs)' that must be navigated to successfully introduce multi-family and mixed-use options.

quotes.text: The majority of zoning in the Catonsville SC area is low density residential, that primarily supports single family development. ... The current residential zoning in the majority of the SC Area does not easily support higher density development.
quotes.briefing_quote: Planning staff emphasized that 'the majority of zoning in the Catonsville Sustainable Community Area is low density residential, which primarily supports single family development' and does not easily accommodate higher density development styles.

quotes.text: Zoning changes occur through the County’s CZMP process... several of these requests for change were denied, though a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144.
quotes.briefing_quote: Recent comprehensive zoning reviews show progress, noting that while some requests were denied, 'a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144' to align with main street commercial revitalization goals.

quotes.text: Support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the SC area through the development process and policy development.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community intends to 'support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the Sustainable Community Area through the development process and policy development' to broaden localized residential choices.

community_organizations: Catonsville, Arbutus, and Edmondson-Westview Recreation Councils

Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Catonsville-Patapsco community envisions a sustainable, well-connected, and culturally vibrant future. Key aspirations include expanding the local arts ecosystem through the newly designated Catonsville Arts and Entertainment District along Frederick Road, improving active transportation and trail connectivity via groups like Catonsville Rails to Trails, and preserving watershed resources near Patapsco Valley State Park. The community aims to revitalize legacy neighborhoods, address commercial vacancies, and expand quality housing choices—including affordable housing partnerships and accessory dwelling units (ADUs)—while navigating existing low-density zoning constraints that historically limit larger-scale infill development.
geographic_addresses: Ingleside Ave & Edmondson Ave, Catonsville, MD
Ingleside Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD

Mellor Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD

quotes.text: Scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger scale new development or infill
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan notes a 'scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger-scale new development or infill,' highlighting the critical importance of strategic infill projects.

quotes.text: Barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs).
quotes.briefing_quote: The assessment identifies clear 'barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs)' that must be navigated to successfully introduce multi-family and mixed-use options.

quotes.text: The majority of zoning in the Catonsville SC area is low density residential, that primarily supports single family development. ... The current residential zoning in the majority of the SC Area does not easily support higher density development.
quotes.briefing_quote: Planning staff emphasized that 'the majority of zoning in the Catonsville Sustainable Community Area is low density residential, which primarily supports single family development' and does not easily accommodate higher density development styles.

quotes.text: Zoning changes occur through the County’s CZMP process... several of these requests for change were denied, though a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144.
quotes.briefing_quote: Recent comprehensive zoning reviews show progress, noting that while some requests were denied, 'a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144' to align with main street commercial revitalization goals.

quotes.text: Support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the SC area through the development process and policy development.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community intends to 'support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the Sustainable Community Area through the development process and policy development' to broaden localized residential choices.

The community aspires to grow through equitable neighborhood development, sustainable transit-oriented design, economic empowerment of local small businesses, environmental and climate justice, and the active preservation of cultural heritage and neighborhood stability.
