plan_quotes.community_vision: Arbutus aspires to transition into a vibrant "college town" leveraging its proximity to the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC) while carefully protecting the area's historic single-family character and small-town charm. The community aims to capitalize on its strategic role as a logistics and technology hub, revitalizing key commercial corridors like East Drive and Linden Avenue with diverse retail, arts, and mixed-use transit-oriented developments that serve residents and students alike.
geographic_addresses: Waelchi Avenue & Sulphur Spring Road, Arbutus, MD
Linden Avenue & Shelbourne Road, Arbutus, MD
Shelbourne Road & Sulphur Spring Road, Arbutus, MD
Tom Day & Southwestern Boulevard, Arbutus, MD

quotes.text: The proposed Arbutus Station is a mixed-use development by a local developer at the intersection of Waelchi Avenue and Sulphur Spring Road. It is within the proposed Sustainable Community boundary and the County's Commercial Revitalization District that can take advantage of the County's revitalization programs if it meets the County revitalization goals and efforts. The project is now submitted for Department's review and approval. The community is actively involved in all development projects in the area to make sure the development fits in with the surrounding area and the project addresses any applicable goals in this plan.
quotes.briefing_quote: With proposals like Arbutus Station at Waelchi Avenue and Sulphur Spring Road, "the community is actively involved in all development projects in the area to make sure the development fits in with the surrounding area and the project addresses any applicable goals in this plan."

quotes.text: Finding a balance between renters and prospective homeowners. Though the community is always looking for prospective homeowners, there is a lack of rental options to attract the UMBC students and programs to benefit both the landlords and student renters. At the same time the community does not want renters to outprice young families moving in and intends to increase homeownership.
quotes.briefing_quote: Workgroup discussions highlighted the challenge of "finding a balance between renters and prospective homeowners," noting that while there is a lack of student rental options, "the community does not want renters to outprice young families moving in and intends to increase homeownership."

quotes.text: Bring diversity in restaurants, quality anchor stores and boutiques similar to Ellicott City and Catonsville.
quotes.briefing_quote: Local economic strategies emphasize the desire to "bring diversity in restaurants, quality anchor stores and boutiques" to the commercial district, modeling success after nearby Ellicott City and Catonsville.

quotes.text: Convene group of design and development professionals to brief community associations on how to rehab and maintain older homes while retaining physical characteristics that add to the charm of the community.
quotes.briefing_quote: To preserve neighborhood character, the plan recommends convening a "group of design and development professionals to brief community associations on how to rehab and maintain older homes while retaining physical characteristics that add to the charm of the community."

quotes.text: Obtain funding and acquire derelict properties to redevelop to meet community needs and UMBC students.
quotes.briefing_quote: To address community health and quality of life, stakeholders recommend seeking funding to "acquire derelict properties to redevelop to meet community needs" and support the growing student population.

community_organizations: Wilkens Police and Community Relations Organization

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Catonsville-Patapsco community envisions a sustainable, well-connected, and culturally vibrant future. Key aspirations include expanding the local arts ecosystem through the newly designated Catonsville Arts and Entertainment District along Frederick Road, improving active transportation and trail connectivity via groups like Catonsville Rails to Trails, and preserving watershed resources near Patapsco Valley State Park. The community aims to revitalize legacy neighborhoods, address commercial vacancies, and expand quality housing choices—including affordable housing partnerships and accessory dwelling units (ADUs)—while navigating existing low-density zoning constraints that historically limit larger-scale infill development.

Ingleside Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD
Maidens Choice Lane & Kenwood Ave, Catonsville, MD
S. Paradise Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD
Mellor Ave & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD
Winters Lane & Frederick Rd, Catonsville, MD

quotes.text: Scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger scale new development or infill
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan notes a 'scarcity of undeveloped properties within residential and commercial zones, thereby limiting the potential for larger-scale new development or infill,' highlighting the critical importance of strategic infill projects.

quotes.text: Barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs).
quotes.briefing_quote: The assessment identifies clear 'barriers to higher density development (including policies, development process, NIMBYs)' that must be navigated to successfully introduce multi-family and mixed-use options.

quotes.text: The majority of zoning in the Catonsville SC area is low density residential, that primarily supports single family development. ... The current residential zoning in the majority of the SC Area does not easily support higher density development.
quotes.briefing_quote: Planning staff emphasized that 'the majority of zoning in the Catonsville Sustainable Community Area is low density residential, which primarily supports single family development' and does not easily accommodate higher density development styles.

quotes.text: Zoning changes occur through the County’s CZMP process... several of these requests for change were denied, though a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144.
quotes.briefing_quote: Recent comprehensive zoning reviews show progress, noting that while some requests were denied, 'a few were approved to allow for mixed uses along MD 144' to align with main street commercial revitalization goals.

quotes.text: Support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the SC area through the development process and policy development.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community intends to 'support the development of new accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within appropriate settings within the Sustainable Community Area through the development process and policy development' to broaden localized residential choices.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Northwest Gateways community seeks to enhance its overall economic vitality, neighborhood livability, and environmental health by pursuing a vision of improved streetscapes, commercial corridor revitalization, and diverse housing options. By leveraging sustainable community programs and targeted public investments, the area strives to foster commercial growth, address transportation and pedestrian connectivity gaps, and build active, safe, and attractive neighborhoods where families of all backgrounds can thrive.

quotes.text: There is currently an affordable housing proposal within the Pikesville CRD that is requesting rezoning to support multi-family apartments.
quotes.briefing_quote: In the Pikesville Commercial Revitalization District, there is an affordable housing proposal requesting rezoning to support multi-family apartments, showing local momentum for adding density.

quotes.text: There has not been demolition of blighted properties in the area. However, there is an interest from the County to assemble vacant commercial properties on Liberty Rd to assist CDCs in redevelopment. In addition, there is discussion to redevelop the old International House of Pancakes and Bennigan's restaurants located in front of Security Square mall.
quotes.briefing_quote: The county is looking to assemble vacant commercial properties along Liberty Road to assist community development corporations in redevelopment, with further discussions centered on redeveloping the former restaurant sites in front of Security Square Mall.

quotes.text: Expand full spectrum housing for residents at diverse income levels and life stages and for individuals with disabilities by encouraging high quality mixed income, multigenerational developments. Promote Housing Accessibility Modification programs to make housing more accessible. Continue to implement smart growth policies by supporting mixed-use development and Traditional Neighborhood Development in the area.
quotes.briefing_quote: Planning guidelines emphasize the need to encourage high-quality mixed-income, multigenerational developments while supporting smart growth policies such as mixed-use and Traditional Neighborhood Development.

quotes.text: Some homes in Colonial Village have been improved. There are homes in the Pikesville area that have gone through the zoning petition process for additions. This is largely attributed to growing families that require additional space and secondary kitchens due to religious food preparation requirements.
quotes.briefing_quote: In Pikesville, growing families are actively seeking zoning petitions for home additions and secondary kitchens to meet specific cultural and religious food preparation needs.

quotes.text: Lack of quality retail and chain restaurants in the Liberty Rd CRD... Lack of variety of businesses to meet the needs of the community... Abundance of unwanted businesses... Businesses closing and vacant gas stations are an eyesore to the residents
quotes.briefing_quote: Community feedback highlights a lack of quality retail and restaurant variety along the Liberty Road Commercial Revitalization District, alongside concerns over vacant storefronts and gas stations.

plan_quotes.community_vision: A Baltimore of harmony, inclusivity, and prosperity, where every child has opportunities to thrive no matter what zip code they live in, and residents play an essential role in Baltimore’s thriving future. The community aspires to grow through equitable neighborhood development, sustainable transit-oriented design, economic empowerment of local small businesses, environmental and climate justice, and the active preservation of cultural heritage and neighborhood stability.
geographic_addresses: 1201 W. Mount Royal Avenue, Baltimore, MD
145 South Calverton Road, Baltimore, MD
1401 East Monument Street, Baltimore, MD
1601 East Lombard Street, Baltimore, MD
Greenmount Avenue & East Chase Street, Baltimore, MD

quotes.text: The Fitzgerald apartment building, located at 1201 W. Mount Royal Avenue in Mid-Town Belvedere, is an example of a successful Transit Oriented Development project in Baltimore. Built in 2010, adjacent to the Mt. Royal/MICA Light Rail station, the seven-story building has 275 apartment units and two commercial establishments on the lower level
quotes.briefing_quote: A prime example of successful transit-oriented development is the Fitzgerald apartment building, which stands as a seven-story building with 275 apartment units and ground-floor commercial establishments adjacent to the Light Rail, showcasing how dense, mixed-use infill can thrive in Baltimore.

quotes.text: In stronger market neighborhoods, it is essential to build affordable housing as part of mixed income developments to affirmatively further fair housing. These areas are relatively rich in the resources needed for quality of life and healthy child development, but as a result of a long practice of exclusion, they currently have limited affordable housing.
quotes.briefing_quote: To affirmatively further fair housing, the plan emphasizes that in stronger market neighborhoods, it is essential to build affordable housing as part of mixed-income developments to reverse long practices of exclusion.

quotes.text: Replacing 629 obsolete public housing units at Perkins Homes and the vacant former Somerset Homes site with over 1,350 units of mixed-income rental housing, a new grocery store, new elementary middle school, two new parks, and a renovated and expanded Chick Webb Recreation Center.

quotes.text: The FLUM focuses new growth into redevelopment areas, which account for approximately 1.5% of the County's already-developed land. This approach addresses high demand for housing and commercial growth.
quotes.briefing_quote: To sustainably manage growth, the plan targets redevelopment on just 1.5% of the County's developed land to balance housing and commercial demands.

quotes.text: Pedestrian safety must be improved—I keep seeing pedestrians walking down the middle of Broken Land or Snowden because there’s no reasonable public transit or walking paths for them to safely get where they’re going.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local workshop participant emphasized that pedestrian safety must be improved on Broken Land Parkway and Snowden River Parkway by providing better walking paths and transit options.

quotes.text: Boosting commercial-base development is one of the most promising strategies to help rebalance the expenditure needs and fiscal resources. The County should continue to build on its current strengths in developing and implementing comprehensive strategies to promote, retain, and expand its commercial base.
quotes.briefing_quote: The Spending Affordability Advisory Committee emphasized that boosting commercial-base development is critical to balancing the County's long-term fiscal resources.

quotes.text: The concept of missing middle housing is referenced throughout the Plan. It is a housing strategy that is intended to create more diverse housing opportunities for our increasingly socioeconomically diverse County.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan promotes missing middle housing to create more diverse housing opportunities that remain compatible in scale with surrounding neighborhoods.

quotes.text: Many developed areas of Howard County are zoned for single-family detached homes. Some of these neighborhoods include homes on larger lots that could, under existing zoning regulations, be further subdivided into one or more additional lots to accommodate a separate home (or homes) of similar size alongside the existing residence.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan identifies potential for modest single-family infill, noting some neighborhoods could be further subdivided under existing zoning to add homes of similar size.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Greater Dundalk/Sparrows Point community envisions a multi-year revitalization strategy focused on increasing economic vitality, expanding environmental resilience, and improving community livability. By leveraging its powerful industrial and deep-water assets like Tradepoint Atlantic and the Port of Baltimore, the community aims to create permanent jobs, expand workforce training, and enhance housing quality. The vision focuses on revitalizing historic commercial corridors like the Historic Dundalk Town Center, preserving waterfront assets, and providing a range of high-quality, affordable housing to support first-time homebuyers and aging-in-place seniors.

quotes.text: Barriers to high density, high-quality development (policies, development approval processes)

This growth is directed away from valuable farmland and sensitive environments, concentrating instead within designated primary growth corridors and community nodes served by central water and sewer systems to maintain the county's rural character, preserve historical resources, and protect the Chesapeake Bay.

quotes.text: Industrial and commercial development should be encouraged to cluster in office parks and employment centers within the Primary Growth Areas as indicated on the Land Use Plan Map (Map 4) They should be well landscaped, buffered from nearby residential areas and should take positive measures to protect sensitive environmental resources.

quotes.text: The High Density Residential (R2) zoning district encompasses only 16.4 acres, or roughly 2.2% of the Town's land area. This zoning district allows for a density of eight (8) dwelling units per acre, permitting townhomes, multi-family dwelling units, two-family dwelling units, and single-family dwelling units. With higher residential densities, future properties zoned R2 should be located in areas with ample transportation access and public facilities to minimize congestion and overloading of existing public infrastructure.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan notes that 'with higher residential densities, future properties zoned R2 should be located in areas with ample transportation access and public facilities to minimize congestion and overloading of existing public infrastructure.'

quotes.text: The Smart Growth Residential (R1-SG) zoning district encompasses 122.8 acres, or roughly 16.8% of the Town's land area. Overall, the R1-SG zoning district is found within the Saber Ridge subdivision on the north end of Town, and within the proposed Quail Run subdivision on the west end of Town. The R1-SG zoning district is comparable to the R1 zoning district; however, the R1-SG zoning district allows for a more compact design with no specified maximum density for residential units and a smaller minimum lot size of 8,000 square feet, whereas the R1 zoning district employs a minimum lot size of 15,000 square feet. This zoning district is unique and should be expanded in future residential housing projects as additional lands are annexed into the Town for development.
quotes.briefing_quote: The Town highlights a sustainable layout strategy, stating that 'the Smart Growth Residential zoning district is unique and should be expanded in future residential housing projects as additional lands are annexed into the Town for development.'

quotes.text: The GC zoning district area is located on the south end of Town along I-70. This district includes more modern-style commercial development with two (2) drive-through restaurants, two (2) gasoline pumping stations, and four (4) tracts of undeveloped commercial land. Most of the Town's future commercial development will likely take place within this district or will be added to this district as adjacent commercial land is annexed into the Town and developed.
quotes.briefing_quote: Planners expect commercial activity to concentrate near major transport nodes, observing that 'most of the Town's future commercial development will likely take place within the General Commercial district or will be added to this district as adjacent commercial land is annexed.'

quotes.text: The Village Center (VC) zoning district is the Town's sole mixed use zoning district, allowing for an array of light commercial and residential uses. The VC zoning district encompasses 73.7 acres, or roughly 10.1% of the Town's land area. The VC zoning district is exclusively found along Main Street in the older areas of the Town developed during a period when individuals lived within close proximity to the Town's central business district (CBD). The Town employed this zoning district to continue to encourage light commercial activities and office space along Main Street while still permitting residential uses.
quotes.briefing_quote: To maintain historic corridor vitality, the plan notes that 'the Town employed the Village Center zoning district to continue to encourage light commercial activities and office space along Main Street while still permitting residential uses.'

Key strategies include overcoming long-standing water capacity constraints through the innovative PUREWater Westminster initiative, expanding high-speed internet via its municipal fiber network, promoting infill and high-density residential developments in the Central and Downtown Business Districts, and creating strategic public-private partnerships to enhance workforce housing and attract new business opportunities.

quotes.text: Promote infill development and other redevelopment options for underutilized residential or commercial lots, and promote the infill of the existing Central Business District and Downtown Business District with business and high density residential uses.
quotes.briefing_quote: To revitalize the commercial core, community planners aim to "promote infill development and other redevelopment options for underutilized residential or commercial lots, and promote the infill of the existing Central Business District and Downtown Business District with business and high density residential uses."

quotes.text: The City approved a market rate 35-unit multi-family apartment complex in 2020.
quotes.briefing_quote: Demonstrating municipal support for rental projects, the plan notes that "the City approved a market rate 35-unit multi-family apartment complex in 2020."

quotes.text: Lack of quality rental housing for workforce population.
quotes.briefing_quote: Westminster housing assessments highlight a strategic opportunity for developers to address a "lack of quality rental housing for workforce population."

quotes.text: The City purchased 17-25 W. Main Street in 2020. The City expects to apply for a demolition grant to remove the existing aging structure in an attempt to attract a developer for a boutique hotel that would attract both local residents and visitors to the City's downtown area.
quotes.briefing_quote: Providing a unique commercial development opportunity, the City seeks to "attract a developer for a boutique hotel that would attract both local residents and visitors to the City's downtown area" at the newly acquired site of 17-25 W. Main Street.

quotes.text: One forward-thinking way the city is planning for the future is by launching PUREWater Westminster, which will use proven technology to purify reclaimed water to provide a safe, sustainable, and drought-resistant drinking water supply. This initiative will help Westminster keep local control of its water supply and costs and provide a pathway for economic growth, business, commercial development, and continued community vitality.
quotes.briefing_quote: To resolve historic utility limitations, the City's PUREWater Westminster infrastructure initiative is designed to "provide a pathway for economic growth, business, commercial development, and continued community vitality."

quotes.text: Continue to build relationships with builders and non-profit developers to increase the affordable housing stock. Partnerships between builders/developers, government, and nonprofit organizations will be key to the production of new for-sale units for low- and moderate-income families.
quotes.briefing_quote: Municipal leaders emphasize their intent to "continue to build relationships with builders and non-profit developers to increase the affordable housing stock" through strategic public-private partnerships.

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.
geographic_addresses: Forge Road & Belair Road, Perry Hall, MD
Compass Road & Wampler Road, Middle River, MD
Cowenton Avenue & Pulaski Highway, White Marsh, MD
Rolling Road & Windsor Mill Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Rolling Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Old Court Road, Randallstown, MD
Wharf Road, Sparrows Point, MD

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

community_organizations: Set the Captives Free Outreach, Worship and Education (OWE) Center

plan_quotes.community_vision: Finksburg's vision centers on the revitalization of its major gateway corridor, focusing on small-scale commercial, office, and retail redevelopment that respects environmental boundaries near the Liberty Reservoir. Since the area lacks public water and sewer, a critical path forward is assessing wastewater options and designing safe, non-motorized bicycle and pedestrian connections away from high-speed state highways, thereby fostering a stronger, more connected community identity.
geographic_addresses: MD 140 & MD 91, Finksburg, MD
Old Westminster Pike, Finksburg, MD
MD 140 & Leidy Road, Finksburg, MD
Dede Road, Finksburg, MD

quotes.text: No public water and sewer; the corridor is dominated by older properties on small lots – many of which do not have room for a replacement septic system. There are development and redevelopment constraints for commercial and residential.
quotes.briefing_quote: Finksburg planning documents note that because there is "no public water and sewer; the corridor is dominated by older properties on small lots – many of which do not have room for a replacement septic system," there are severe development and redevelopment constraints for both commercial and residential projects.

quotes.text: Encouraging redevelopment as a way to promote new small-scale businesses, offices, and retail activity within the corridor is a goal of the Finksburg Corridor Plan (2013).
quotes.briefing_quote: To spark economic renewal, county planning guidelines highlight that "encouraging redevelopment as a way to promote new small-scale businesses, offices, and retail activity within the corridor" is a central goal for the Finksburg area.

quotes.text: A goal of the Finksburg Corridor Plan (2013) is to provide opportunities for residential uses along secondary roadways that are compatible in design and density with the historic structures and the existing community character.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community legacy goals emphasize preserving local character, aiming "to provide opportunities for residential uses along secondary roadways that are compatible in design and density with the historic structures and the existing community character."

quotes.text: Old Westminster Pike is underutilized and provides the opportunity for economic and social revitalization as a commercial and community activity center servicing the area’s residential population and the future commercial needs of the neighborhood.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights that "Old Westminster Pike is underutilized and provides the opportunity for economic and social revitalization as a commercial and community activity center" to serve both existing residents and future business needs.

quotes.text: Public water and sewer is not currently available in the SC, so zoning and density are limited by septic laws.
quotes.briefing_quote: Wastewater infrastructure remains a critical barrier, as "public water and sewer is not currently available in the Sustainable Community, so zoning and density are limited by septic laws."

plan_quotes.community_vision: Montgomery County aspires to transition from a suburban bedroom community into an interconnected, economically competitive, and racially integrated jurisdiction. The county's vision centers on compact, corridor-focused development that fosters walkable 'Complete Communities' and '15-minute living' while preserving its Agricultural Reserve. The plan prioritizes addressing historical racial and economic inequities, improving environmental resilience, and integrating design, arts, and culture into the daily lives of all residents.
geographic_addresses: 2425 Reedie Drive, Wheaton, MD
Connecticut Avenue & Manor Road, Kensington, MD
University Boulevard & New Hampshire Avenue, Silver Spring, MD
Seven Locks Road & River Road, Bethesda, MD

quotes.text: The establishment of the residential wedge consigned more than one-third of the county to zoning exclusively for single-family homes, leaving many of our neighborhoods reliant on automobiles and disconnected from many amenities and services.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights that dedicating more than one-third of the county to exclusive single-family zoning left many neighborhoods isolated, signaling a key opportunity to introduce missing middle housing and mixed-use options that better connect residents to daily amenities.

quotes.text: By concentrating more housing of different sizes and types near high-quality transit corridors, we can provide housing that will help keep the most productive workers in the county, curb escalating prices in the most desirable locations, and improve accessibility of jobs, transportation, and services while being mindful not to displace current residents.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support a growing workforce, planning officials recommend concentrating more housing of different sizes and types near high-quality transit corridors to keep housing attainable, improve transit access, and avoid displacement.

quotes.text: Existing suburban office parks in locations such as Rock Spring or Clarksburg’s COMSAT site have large existing buildings that can accommodate employment but lack the integration of uses, services, and amenities necessary to succeed in an increasingly competitive office market.
quotes.briefing_quote: The document notes that aging suburban office parks can be successfully repositioned through infill and redevelopment to integrate housing, retail, and public spaces, creating the vibrant mixed-use environments that modern employers and residents seek.

quotes.text: Adding more 'Missing Middle' housing types – ranging from low to medium densities such as accessory dwelling units (ADUs); duplexes; triplexes; quadplexes; live-work units; and clustered housing such as townhouses, courtyard dwellings and smaller apartment buildings to more neighborhoods is intended to provide more choice, enhance intergenerational interaction, promote aging in place, and build social capital.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan emphasizes the value of adding 'Missing Middle' housing types to more neighborhoods—including duplexes, triplexes, and townhomes—to expand residential choice, build social capital, and facilitate aging in place.

quotes.text: Can't take my ladder on the Purple Line.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local working-class resident cautioned planners about transit-focused changes, stating, 'Can’t take my ladder on the Purple Line,' illustrating the critical need to preserve vehicle-accessible corridors and parking for service providers.

The community aspires to grow through equitable neighborhood development, sustainable transit-oriented design, economic empowerment of local small businesses, environmental and climate justice, and the active preservation of cultural heritage and neighborhood stability.

quotes.text: The Fitzgerald apartment building, located at 1201 W. Mount Royal Avenue in Mid-Town Belvedere, is an example of a successful Transit Oriented Development project in Baltimore. Built in 2010, adjacent to the Mt. Royal/MICA Light Rail station, the seven-story building has 275 apartment units and two commercial establishments on the lower level
quotes.briefing_quote: A prime example of successful transit-oriented development is the Fitzgerald apartment building, which stands as a seven-story building with 275 apartment units and ground-floor commercial establishments adjacent to the Light Rail, showcasing how dense, mixed-use infill can thrive in Baltimore.

quotes.text: In stronger market neighborhoods, it is essential to build affordable housing as part of mixed income developments to affirmatively further fair housing. These areas are relatively rich in the resources needed for quality of life and healthy child development, but as a result of a long practice of exclusion, they currently have limited affordable housing.
quotes.briefing_quote: To affirmatively further fair housing, the plan emphasizes that in stronger market neighborhoods, it is essential to build affordable housing as part of mixed-income developments to reverse long practices of exclusion.

quotes.text: Replacing 629 obsolete public housing units at Perkins Homes and the vacant former Somerset Homes site with over 1,350 units of mixed-income rental housing, a new grocery store, new elementary middle school, two new parks, and a renovated and expanded Chick Webb Recreation Center.
quotes.briefing_quote: The Perkins Somerset Oldtown Transformation Plan represents a massive revitalization effort, replacing obsolete housing with over 1,350 units of mixed-income rental housing, a new grocery store, and essential community spaces.

quotes.text: These homes generate wealth over generations for many families whose future security is inextricably tied to their communities’ ongoing success. These are largely stable, highly livable, and resilient communities, but unfortunately, they have historically received little benefit from national and local housing policies that have often failed to support the middle class.
quotes.briefing_quote: Housing policy experts highlighted the critical need to support middle neighborhoods, noting that these homes generate wealth over generations for families whose future security is tied to their communities' ongoing success.

quotes.text: Despite gains in income, the City continues to experience a shortage of affordable rental and homeownership units particularly for households earning 50% or less of the Area Median Income (AMI) as determined by the U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development (HUD).
quotes.briefing_quote: The 2023 Sustainable Communities report underscores that despite general income gains, Baltimore "continues to experience a shortage of affordable rental and homeownership units particularly for households earning 50% or less of the Area Median Income."

quotes.text: Each district’s Main Street program has a different strategy for spurring economic activity, but support may include marketing and event planning, financial assistance for design and promotions, architectural services for facade renovations, streetscape improvements, technical support, access to grants, and more to support the City’s eight (8) Main Street Districts.
quotes.briefing_quote: To revitalize local business hubs, Main Street program strategies include offering "financial assistance for design and promotions, architectural services for facade renovations, and streetscape improvements" to draw in new commercial tenants.

quotes.text: Yard 56, a former industrial site redeveloped as a mixed-use development across from Hopkins Bayview.
quotes.briefing_quote: Opportunity Zone initiatives have catalyzed key transformations, such as "Yard 56, a former industrial site redeveloped as a mixed-use development across from Hopkins Bayview."

quotes.text: To provide safe and decent housing and help owners maintain their housing values, the City and Housing Authority dedicate considerable resources to increasing and preserving its supply of affordable housing for both homeowners and renters.
quotes.briefing_quote: Municipal planners indicated that the city aims to "dedicate considerable resources to increasing and preserving its supply of affordable housing for both homeowners and renters" to stabilize residential neighborhoods.

quotes.text: Vacant lots and buildings are consolidated to create new mixed-income rental and for-sale housing sites. Abandoned industrial sites are repurposed and frequently leverage additional investment.
quotes.briefing_quote: By optimizing municipal land assets, "vacant lots and buildings are consolidated to create new mixed-income rental and for-sale housing sites" that spark wider neighborhood investment.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The City of Frederick's vision, driven by its CommUNITY 2030 Strategic Plan and 2020 Comprehensive Plan, focuses on sustainable, equitable development across three distinct corridors: Downtown, the Golden Mile, and East Frederick. The community seeks to revitalize underutilized commercial areas and preserve its historic character through selective redevelopment, adaptive reuse, and strategic infill. Key goals include diversifying and increasing housing options (especially affordable and multi-family residential units), enhancing multi-modal transportation systems with shared-use paths, implementing form-based codes to encourage vibrant mixed-use environments, and fostering robust public-private collaborations to ensure high quality of life for all residents.

quotes.text: The majority of the existing strip centers give little regard for efficiently integrated vehicular and pedestrian access. quotes.text: The TB district effectively prohibits the mixing of residential uses with commercial uses and thus prevents building owners from adapting to market conditions that favor residential.

quotes.text: The Zoning Ordinance effectively prohibits the creation of most housing types that could meet the needs and preference of people who would like to live in or near a historic downtown. It also prevents the conversion of long vacant storefronts into needed housing.

quotes.text: Some intensification of existing areas may be feasible but additional space for modern light industrial and office employment is necessary to capitalize again on regional economic development.

quotes.text: Open lands in and around the Town could be developed as conventional single-use residential subdivisions or in ways that distinguish them as excellent neighborhoods unique to Thurmont. quotes.briefing_quote: Rather than allowing conventional subdivisions, the plan calls for deliberate coordination, warning that 'left to chance, land development seldom organizes itself into coherent extensions of existing or historic patterns' and highlighting the opportunity to design exceptional, integrated neighborhoods.

quotes.text: Within and near Downtown, mixed-use development is encouraged as well as a broad array of land uses including the commercial uses that exist there today and a variety of housing types such as apartment and condominium buildings, senior housing, and townhouses.

quotes.text: Improve local connectivity through dedicated bus lanes, new cross easements between shopping centers, and introduction of mixed-use development

quotes.text: Sustain the vitality of Downtown Frederick by promoting adaptive reuse/redevelopment of underutilized properties and strategic infill developments
quotes.briefing_quote: Planning documents highlight the goal to "sustain the vitality of Downtown Frederick by promoting adaptive reuse/redevelopment of underutilized properties and strategic infill developments" to meet modern housing and economic needs.

quotes.text: Ensure flexible land use regulations to allow suitable mixtures of residential and non-residential uses within new and existing development
quotes.briefing_quote: The City aims to "ensure flexible land use regulations to allow suitable mixtures of residential and non-residential uses" within both new and existing developments.

quotes.text: Consider creating an Affordable Housing Fund with a dedicated stream of revenue. For example, tax rental units owned by non-City residents at a higher rate and place the difference in the AHF to discourage investors from buying up properties within the City.

The City intends to manage sustainable urban development that balances economic prosperity with housing, employment, and cultural opportunities for everyone. Through active civic engagement, Frederick aims to strengthen its vibrant downtown and diverse, walkable neighborhoods, supported by well-coordinated, multimodal transportation choices that connect residents locally and regionally.

quotes.text: The rise in population has resulted in the developments and investments in newly annexed lands, along with denser and compact infill development in and around the downtown core.

quotes.text: Except for the Downtown area, the majority of the City’s residential neighborhoods are characterized by lower densities, wider streets, and uniformity in the types of structures and styles. quotes.text: One of the concerns consistently stressed by residents is the segregation of land uses and the lack of nearby supporting retail and service uses. This segregation of land uses contributes to an increase in the length and number of automobile trips.
quotes.briefing_quote: During public workshops, citizens consistently voiced concern regarding 'the segregation of land uses and the lack of nearby supporting retail and service uses,' urging the City to encourage mixed-use neighborhoods to reduce dependency on cars.

quotes.text: The majority of the existing strip centers give little regard for efficiently integrated vehicular and pedestrian access. quotes.briefing_quote: The plan emphasizes that 'the majority of the existing strip centers give little regard for efficiently integrated vehicular and pedestrian access,' recommending that future commercial corridor redevelopments tie seamlessly back into surrounding neighborhoods.

quotes.text: The residential land uses are proposed at greater densities than previously approved by City Comprehensive Plans. The purpose of this is to provide incentives towards infill and redevelopment and to encourage a higher population served by existing services and utilities.
quotes.briefing_quote: To leverage existing infrastructure, 'residential land uses are proposed at greater densities than previously approved' to incentivize urban infill and support a growing downtown customer base.

quotes.text: Consider zoning standards that would allow neighborhoods with a mix of housing types and sizes that can accommodate a variety of households, including renters and owners.

quotes.text: Seek partners and funding to increase the supply of housing for the senior population, including developments that support aging in place.
quotes.briefing_quote: To address demographic shifts, the plan highlights an opportunity to 'seek partners and funding to increase the supply of housing for the senior population, including developments that support aging in place.'

quotes.text: Permit apartments in Old Town and B-1 Neighborhood Business districts, as well as the R-3 and R-4 Residential districts.
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan encourages expanding density in commercial nodes by recommending policies to 'permit apartments in Old Town and Neighborhood Business districts, as well as the R-3 and R-4 Residential districts.'

quotes.text: Review and amend the Zoning Ordinance requirements to permit accessory dwelling units and tiny houses, and develop criteria and conditions for their approval.
quotes.briefing_quote: To encourage creative housing options, the town aims to 'review and amend the Zoning Ordinance requirements to permit accessory dwelling units and tiny houses, and develop criteria and conditions for their approval.'

quotes.text: The LI and LIP district regulations should be reviewed to refocus the districts on wholesaling, warehousing, limited manufacturing and assembly uses, offices, research laboratories and other employment uses.
quotes.briefing_quote: To stimulate local economic development, the plan indicates that 'the Limited Industrial and Limited Industrial Park district regulations should be reviewed to refocus the districts on wholesaling, warehousing, limited manufacturing and assembly uses, offices, research laboratories and other employment uses.'

quotes.text: The B-1 zoning stated purpose and intent is "to encourage the provision of small, safe, attractive and well-located shopping areas for primarily pedestrian use in a manner that will make them compatible assets to the residential environment."
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights that the Neighborhood Business zoning intends 'to encourage the provision of small, safe, attractive and well-located shopping areas for primarily pedestrian use' as compatible assets to the neighborhood.

quotes.text: Adaptive reuse of old commercial/industrial structures can be difficult due to lack of flexibility of the zoning code.

quotes.text: When asked what types of development they would like to see more of in Walkersville, restaurants and neighborhood business were cited most frequently (by nearly 70% and 47% of respondents, respectively).

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

The community aims to capitalize on its strategic role as a logistics and technology hub, revitalizing key commercial corridors like East Drive and Linden Avenue with diverse retail, arts, and mixed-use transit-oriented developments that serve residents and students alike.

quotes.text: The proposed Arbutus Station is a mixed-use development by a local developer at the intersection of Waelchi Avenue and Sulphur Spring Road. It is within the proposed Sustainable Community boundary and the County's Commercial Revitalization District that can take advantage of the County's revitalization programs if it meets the County revitalization goals and efforts. The project is now submitted for Department's review and approval. The community is actively involved in all development projects in the area to make sure the development fits in with the surrounding area and the project addresses any applicable goals in this plan.
quotes.briefing_quote: With proposals like Arbutus Station at Waelchi Avenue and Sulphur Spring Road, "the community is actively involved in all development projects in the area to make sure the development fits in with the surrounding area and the project addresses any applicable goals in this plan."

quotes.text: Finding a balance between renters and prospective homeowners. Though the community is always looking for prospective homeowners, there is a lack of rental options to attract the UMBC students and programs to benefit both the landlords and student renters. At the same time the community does not want renters to outprice young families moving in and intends to increase homeownership.
quotes.briefing_quote: Workgroup discussions highlighted the challenge of "finding a balance between renters and prospective homeowners," noting that while there is a lack of student rental options, "the community does not want renters to outprice young families moving in and intends to increase homeownership."

quotes.text: Bring diversity in restaurants, quality anchor stores and boutiques similar to Ellicott City and Catonsville.
quotes.briefing_quote: Local economic strategies emphasize the desire to "bring diversity in restaurants, quality anchor stores and boutiques" to the commercial district, modeling success after nearby Ellicott City and Catonsville.

quotes.text: Convene group of design and development professionals to brief community associations on how to rehab and maintain older homes while retaining physical characteristics that add to the charm of the community.
quotes.briefing_quote: To preserve neighborhood character, the plan recommends convening a "group of design and development professionals to brief community associations on how to rehab and maintain older homes while retaining physical characteristics that add to the charm of the community."

quotes.text: Obtain funding and acquire derelict properties to redevelop to meet community needs and UMBC students.
quotes.briefing_quote: To address community health and quality of life, stakeholders recommend seeking funding to "acquire derelict properties to redevelop to meet community needs" and support the growing student population.

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Town of Centreville aims to guide its growth through 2040 by balancing careful development with the conservation of its unique small-town character, historic assets, and natural resources. The community envisions a transition toward ecologically sustainable complete neighborhoods that incorporate a variety of housing options, walkable streets, and interconnected open spaces and greenways. Simultaneously, the Town seeks to expand its municipal water and wastewater systems, foster a resilient commercial tax base through a new Technology Enterprise District, and ensure its downtown remains a vibrant, walkable center of civic and economic life.

quotes.text: The Plan also encourages residential apartments above commercial storefronts and new residential buildings with densities that can meaningfully increase the resident population in the CBD, such as one housing unit per 1,200 square feet of lot area. The Plan recommends that the Zoning Ordinance be amended to allow standalone residential building within the CBD.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support downtown vitality, the plan encourages "residential apartments above commercial storefronts and new residential buildings" with densities that can meaningfully increase the resident population in the Central Business District, recommending zoning amendments to allow standalone residential buildings.

quotes.text: In the future, homes may be clustered in higher density arrangements and in attached buildings which will leave more open space to be preserved. Housing types and architecture are likely to be different than they are today too, and zoning, subdivision, and infrastructure standards may need to be modified to guide development where energy efficiency, affordability, and very economical utility delivery will be driving forces in community design.
quotes.briefing_quote: Looking toward 2040, the plan anticipates that "homes may be clustered in higher density arrangements and in attached buildings" to preserve open space, necessitating modifications to zoning, subdivision, and infrastructure standards to support energy efficiency and affordability.

quotes.text: Another common development pattern that is not intended to occur in the Growth Areas is large lot suburban sprawl that consumes inordinate amounts of land without the provision of open space, community character, and linkage to the core of Centreville.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community intends to move away from conventional patterns, noting that "large lot suburban sprawl that consumes inordinate amounts of land" is not desired, focusing instead on providing open space, community character, and strong linkages to the core of Centreville.

quotes.text: This Plan recommends the creation of a Technology Enterprise District (TED) to be reserved for master developed and cohesively planned projects. Nearly 135 acres are so designated for office and light industrial use. quotes.text: Expanding the areas where multi-family and apartment development is allowed would increase the availability of development sites and reduce the cost of land per unit. The County and municipalities should review and increase allowable densities where appropriate.

quotes.text: By reducing the growth of new residential development in agricultural and rural areas... encouraging and directing growth to existing communities and within designated areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: The county's primary growth management strategy focuses on "reducing the growth of new residential development in agricultural and rural areas" by directing future growth into established communities.

quotes.text: In the Grasonville Village Center, low- and medium-intensity commercial uses are encouraged, along with single-family and multi-family housing. The existing village scale is maintained and enhanced so that this area once again becomes a true village center...
quotes.briefing_quote: For the Grasonville Village Center, the plan outlines an opportunity where "low- and medium-intensity commercial uses are encouraged, along with single-family and multi-family housing" to help reestablish a vibrant village scale.

quotes.text: It is the County's intent that remaining un-allocated sewer capacity should be reserved for commercial uses, directing any new residential development to the incorporated towns that have capacity to accommodate it. Infill development is development that takes place on vacant, undeveloped or underutilized parcels within an area that is already characterized by development...
quotes.briefing_quote: To address infrastructure constraints, the plan stresses the need to "reserve remaining sewer capacity for commercial uses, directing any new residential development to the incorporated towns" that have the capacity to accommodate it.

quotes.text: Many communities are making zoning provisions for 'Missing Middle' housing—housing types with unit sizes and densities between those of single-family and multi-family zones... They include small-lot single-family units, duplexes, triplexes, townhouses, cottage homes, and small multi-family buildings of four to eight units.
quotes.briefing_quote: To provide more diverse and affordable choices, the plan encourages zoning provisions for "'Missing Middle' housing—housing types with unit sizes and densities between those of single-family and multi-family zones".

quotes.text: The Centreville water service map also shows an area designated as W-3 at the intersection of US 301/MD 304. It was suggested that the vacant areas be developed into a County-developed business park.
quotes.briefing_quote: The planning framework identifies a strategic opportunity at the intersection of US 301 and MD 304 to develop vacant agricultural parcels into a County-developed business park, supporting a balanced mix of commercial, industrial, and municipal uses.

quotes.text: Both the Town and County Comprehensive Plans call for a mix of residential and commercial land uses on lands in and adjacent to the Town and within the Queenstown Growth Area.
quotes.briefing_quote: Comprehensive strategies for Queenstown emphasize the need to integrate a balanced mix of residential and commercial land uses within the designated growth area to foster vibrant local development.

quotes.text: TRUE commercial apartments – zoning may need to be refined such that the apartments would be ancillary to the commercial, not the other way around.

quotes.text: Prohibit any further large-scale residential development. Remove large vacant parcels from the Growth Area – rezone/downzone if required

plan_quotes.community_vision: The Town of Sudlersville is eager to embrace smart growth and green practices to expand responsibly at a sustainable rate while preserving its historic character. Through key initiatives like the creation of a community center in a revitalized school building, streetscape improvements, and flexible zoning updates (such as floating zones and Planned Neighborhood Development), the town aims to increase its marketability to area businesses, attract new residents, and provide diverse housing options for its growing senior population.
geographic_addresses: 200 South Church Street, Sudlersville, MD
Maple Street, Sudlersville, MD

quotes.text: To deter barriers of Smart Growth, the Town has updated its Zoning Ordinance to allow for floating zones and Planned Neighborhood Development. This allows for flexible zoning to accommodate mixed use or denser development. The updated Zoning Ordinance also allows mixed use in the Town Center district, commercial on the first floor, and residential on the second floor.
quotes.briefing_quote: To lower barriers to smart growth, town administrators highlighted that the town has updated its Zoning Ordinance to allow for floating zones and Planned Neighborhood Development, allowing for "flexible zoning to accommodate mixed use or denser development," including first-floor commercial and second-floor residential options in the Town Center.

quotes.text: The MU District is intended to provide for higher intensity non-residential uses in the existing light industrial and heavier commercial areas of Town and in some adjacent potential annexation areas. A limited amount of higher density residential uses are also appropriate. Mixed uses are encouraged.
quotes.briefing_quote: The town's Mixed Use (MU) District guidelines encourage creative growth by specifying that "a limited amount of higher density residential uses are also appropriate" alongside higher intensity non-residential uses in light industrial and heavy commercial areas.

quotes.text: The TR District is intended to preserve and protect the Town's traditional primarily residential neighborhoods and allow certain non-residential uses that are compatible with residential character, and to encourage and facilitate redevelopment and infill that is compatible in use, scale, and impact with residential uses and the existing pattern of buildings, streets and blocks.
quotes.briefing_quote: In the Town Residential (TR) District, the planning framework aims to protect neighborhoods while encouraging developers to "facilitate redevelopment and infill that is compatible in use, scale, and impact with residential uses" and the existing community fabric.

quotes.text: This would allow for a previously abandoned building to be revitalized, providing a community center as well as possibly veteran apartments and office space.
quotes.briefing_quote: Highlighting adaptive reuse opportunities, town representatives identified a project that would revitalize an abandoned school building to provide "a community center as well as possibly veteran apartments and office space."

quotes.text: The future development of the annexed property will increase job creations due to the portion allocated as industrial zoning. The annexed area is approximately 300 acres. We would like to put a plan in place to solicit businesses for this industrial.
quotes.briefing_quote: Looking toward future economic expansion, planning materials state that a proposed 300-acre annexation includes a portion allocated for industrial zoning, with a goal to "solicit businesses for this industrial" area to boost local job creation.

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

quotes.text: These homes generate wealth over generations for many families whose future security is inextricably tied to their communities’ ongoing success. The goal is to stimulate economic growth, enhance recreational parks and green spaces, expand diverse and affordable housing options—including mixed-use development and accessory dwelling units—and build organizational capacity through a new community development organization to champion local reinvestment.

Harford Road & Putty Hill Avenue, Parkville, MD
Belair Road & Dunfield Road, Overlea, MD

quotes.text: Identify potential zoning changes to encourage the development of high-quality, mixed-use development along major corridors in the Sustainable Community area.
quotes.briefing_quote: To spur revitalization, county planners proposed to "identify potential zoning changes to encourage the development of high-quality, mixed-use development along major corridors in the Sustainable Community area."

quotes.text: Provide funding and support to the creation of additional affordable housing units in the Sustainable Community area, including at the existing Days Inn property in the Joppa Road corridor.
quotes.briefing_quote: The community plans to "provide funding and support to the creation of additional affordable housing units in the Sustainable Community area, including at the existing Days Inn property in the Joppa Road corridor."

quotes.text: Support the development of accessory dwelling units within appropriate settings within the SC area through the development process and policy development
quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights a strategy to "support the development of accessory dwelling units within appropriate settings within the Sustainable Community area through the development process and policy development."

quotes.text: Provide suitable incentives for key redevelopments of aging commercial and multi-family properties in the Hillendale, Parkville, and Overlea area.
quotes.briefing_quote: Revitalization efforts seek to "provide suitable incentives for key redevelopments of aging commercial and multi-family properties in the Hillendale, Parkville, and Overlea area."

quotes.text: Identify opportunities for appropriate changes in current zoning to allow for the incorporation of additional residential units into existing residential structures and areas
quotes.briefing_quote: To diversify local options, planners aim to "identify opportunities for appropriate changes in current zoning to allow for the incorporation of additional residential units into existing residential structures and areas."

plan_quotes.community_vision: Baltimore County envisions a future centered on creating livable, healthy, and equitable communities in harmony with nature, supported by a resilient economy and strong regional partnerships. Facing a depletion of undeveloped greenfield land inside the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL), the County is shifting its growth strategy toward retrofitting and redevelopment. This approach focuses density, walkability, public spaces, and mixed-use developments into designated 'Nodes'—such as aging commercial centers, transit stations, and greyfields—while steadfastly preserving the agricultural and natural resources of its rural areas.
geographic_addresses: Forge Road & Belair Road, Perry Hall, MD
Compass Road & Wampler Road, Middle River, MD
Cowenton Avenue & Pulaski Highway, White Marsh, MD
Rolling Road & Windsor Mill Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Rolling Road, Windsor Mill, MD
Liberty Road & Old Court Road, Randallstown, MD
Wharf Road, Sparrows Point, MD

quotes.text: The availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development in areas within the Urban Rural Demarcation Line (URDL); our water and sewer infrastructure are aging; our transit system needs modernization; our housing supply struggles to meet demand; and our commercial areas require a different perspective than what was used in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: The County Council's opening statement highlighted that "the availability of developable land in the County continues to be a challenge, particularly for in-fill development... and our housing supply struggles to meet demand," underscoring the vital need for modern infill and mixed-use approaches.

quotes.text: The County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles—walking, biking and public transit.
quotes.briefing_quote: Members of the Green Towson Alliance noted that "the County should make every effort to plan for [anticipated] growth by offering multiple forms of mobility other than automobiles," advocating for ped-friendly, transit-oriented mixed-use developments.

quotes.text: There's not a whole lot of land inside the URDL that can have traditional suburban developments, so we need to move towards high standard high-density developments. This is different than the construction/development that has occurred in the past.
quotes.briefing_quote: A workshop participant observed that since traditional suburban land is nearly depleted inside the boundary, "we need to move towards high standard high-density developments" rather than continuing legacy sprawl patterns.

quotes.text: We want more diversity in the business types in retail areas.
quotes.briefing_quote: Owings Mills community members expressed that they "want more diversity in the business types in retail areas," indicating a local push to revitalize and diversify aging retail strips.

quotes.text: Create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development in and near transit stations by utilizing a Smart Growth framework.
quotes.briefing_quote: To support sustainable growth, the plan recommends to "create new and adjust existing overlay districts with implementation tools and incentives to encourage walkable, mixed-use development" near transit hubs.

quotes.text: The Planned Unit Development (PUD) Process should be evaluated and updated.
quotes.briefing_quote: A local resident noted during the public comment phase that "the Planned Unit Development process should be evaluated and updated" to ensure higher quality development, transparency, and explicit community benefits.

community_organizations: Set the Captives Free Outreach, Worship and Education (OWE) Center

plan_quotes.community_vision: A Baltimore of harmony, inclusivity, and prosperity, where every child has opportunities to thrive no matter what zip code they live in, and residents play an essential role in Baltimore’s thriving future. The community aspires to grow through equitable neighborhood development, sustainable transit-oriented design, economic empowerment of local small businesses, environmental and climate justice, and the active preservation of cultural heritage and neighborhood stability.

quotes.text: The Fitzgerald apartment building, located at 1201 W. Mount Royal Avenue in Mid-Town Belvedere, is an example of a successful Transit Oriented Development project in Baltimore. Built in 2010, adjacent to the Mt. Royal/MICA Light Rail station, the seven-story building has 275 apartment units and two commercial establishments on the lower level
quotes.briefing_quote: A prime example of successful transit-oriented development is the Fitzgerald apartment building, which stands as a seven-story building with 275 apartment units and ground-floor commercial establishments adjacent to the Light Rail, showcasing how dense, mixed-use infill can thrive in Baltimore.

quotes.text: In stronger market neighborhoods, it is essential to build affordable housing as part of mixed income developments to affirmatively further fair housing. These areas are relatively rich in the resources needed for quality of life and healthy child development, but as a result of a long practice of exclusion, they currently have limited affordable housing.
quotes.briefing_quote: To affirmatively further fair housing, the plan emphasizes that in stronger market neighborhoods, it is essential to build affordable housing as part of mixed-income developments to reverse long practices of exclusion.

quotes.text: Replacing 629 obsolete public housing units at Perkins Homes and the vacant former Somerset Homes site with over 1,350 units of mixed-income rental housing, a new grocery store, new elementary middle school, two new parks, and a renovated and expanded Chick Webb Recreation Center.
quotes.briefing_quote: The Perkins Somerset Oldtown Transformation Plan represents a massive revitalization effort, replacing obsolete housing with over 1,350 units of mixed-income rental housing, a new grocery store, and essential community spaces.

quotes.text: These homes generate wealth over generations for many families whose future security is inextricably tied to their communities’ ongoing success. These are largely stable, highly livable, and resilient communities, but unfortunately, they have historically received little benefit from national and local housing policies that have often failed to support the middle class.
quotes.briefing_quote: Housing policy experts highlighted the critical need to support middle neighborhoods, noting that these homes generate wealth over generations for families whose future security is tied to their communities' ongoing success.

quotes.text: Despite gains in income, the City continues to experience a shortage of affordable rental and homeownership units particularly for households earning 50% or less of the Area Median Income (AMI) as determined by the U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development (HUD).
quotes.briefing_quote: The 2023 Sustainable Communities report underscores that despite general income gains, Baltimore "continues to experience a shortage of affordable rental and homeownership units particularly for households earning 50% or less of the Area Median Income."

quotes.text: Each district’s Main Street program has a different strategy for spurring economic activity, but support may include marketing and event planning, financial assistance for design and promotions, architectural services for facade renovations, streetscape improvements, technical support, access to grants, and more to support the City’s eight (8) Main Street Districts.
quotes.briefing_quote: To revitalize local business hubs, Main Street program strategies include offering "financial assistance for design and promotions, architectural services for facade renovations, and streetscape improvements" to draw in new commercial tenants.

quotes.text: Yard 56, a former industrial site redeveloped as a mixed-use development across from Hopkins Bayview.
quotes.briefing_quote: Opportunity Zone initiatives have catalyzed key transformations, such as "Yard 56, a former industrial site redeveloped as a mixed-use development across from Hopkins Bayview."

quotes.text: To provide safe and decent housing and help owners maintain their housing values, the City and Housing Authority dedicate considerable resources to increasing and preserving its supply of affordable housing for both homeowners and renters.
quotes.briefing_quote: Municipal planners indicated that the city aims to "dedicate considerable resources to increasing and preserving its supply of affordable housing for both homeowners and renters" to stabilize residential neighborhoods.

quotes.text: Vacant lots and buildings are consolidated to create new mixed-income rental and for-sale housing sites. Abandoned industrial sites are repurposed and frequently leverage additional investment.
quotes.briefing_quote: By optimizing municipal land assets, "vacant lots and buildings are consolidated to create new mixed-income rental and for-sale housing sites" that spark wider neighborhood investment.
